record.original_question: What is a complete characterization of solid bricks, where a brick is a nonbipartite matching covered graph with no nontrivial tight cuts and a matching covered graph is solid when every separating cut is tight? Equivalently for bricks, which nonbipartite matching covered graphs are free of nontrivial separating cuts, and what is the computational complexity of deciding from a given brick whether it is solid? In particular, is this decision problem in NP, and is it solvable in polynomial time?

evidence.quote: A matching covered graph is solid if every separating cut of G is a tight cut.
Solid bricks are precisely those bricks which are free of nontrivial separating cuts.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. Let $G$ be a finite simple connected graph with at least one perfect matching. An edge of $G$ is called admissible if some perfect matching of $G$ contains it. The graph $G$ is matching covered if every edge of $G$ is admissible.

For a vertex set $X \subseteq V(G)$ with $\emptyset \neq X \neq V(G)$, the cut $C := \partial(X) = \{uv \in E(G) : u \in X, v \notin X\}$ has shores $X$ and $V(G) \setminus X$. The cut $C$ is trivial if one of its shores is a single vertex. The cut-contractions $G/X$ and $G/(V(G)\setminus X)$ are obtained from $G$ by contracting each shore to a single vertex (deleting any resulting loops).

A cut $C = \partial(X)$ is tight if $|M \cap C| = 1$ for every perfect matching $M$ of $G$. A cut $C$ is separating if both cut-contractions $G/X$ and $G/(V(G)\setminus X)$ are themselves matching covered. (Every tight cut is separating.) The graph $G$ is solid if every separating cut of $G$ is a tight cut.

A brick is a non-bipartite matching covered graph that has no nontrivial tight cut. For bricks, being solid is equivalent to having no nontrivial separating cut.

Problems. 
(a) Give a complete structural characterization of solid bricks: describe, in graph-theoretic terms, exactly which non-bipartite matching covered graphs without nontrivial tight cuts have the property that they also have no nontrivial separating cut.
(b) Determine the computational complexity of the decision problem SOLID BRICK: given a brick $G$, decide whether $G$ is solid. In particular, is SOLID BRICK in NP? Is SOLID BRICK in P?
artifact.status_search_result: The problem of characterizing solid bricks and determining the complexity of recognizing them remains open. Recent work (e.g., a 2025 paper characterizing claw-free solid bricks and other structural results on subclasses) explicitly states that a complete characterization of solid bricks is unknown and that the complexity of deciding whether a brick is solid is not known to be in NP or in P.

status_evidence.title: Claw-Free Solid Bricks
status_evidence.snippet: Solid bricks have many interesting properties, but the complexity of determining whether a given brick is solid remains unknown. We characterize all the claw-free solid bricks.
status_evidence.claim: As of 2025, the complexity of recognizing solid bricks is still unknown, and only restricted subclasses (e.g., claw-free) have been characterized.

status_evidence.title: On Two Unsolved Problems Concerning Matching Covered Graphs
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses unsolved problems on matching covered graphs including solid brick characterization.
status_evidence.claim: Solid brick characterization is an unsolved problem in matching theory.

status_evidence.title: Wheel-like bricks and minimal matching covered graphs
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses solid bricks as components in structural analysis but does not resolve the characterization or recognition complexity.
status_evidence.claim: Recent (2024) literature continues to treat solid brick characterization as an open structural problem.
